claim: The nitrogenase Fe protein mediates ATP-dependent electron transfer to the nitrogenase MoFe protein during nitrogen fixation.
source: The nitrogenase Fe protein mediates ATP-dependent electron transfer to the nitrogenase MoFe protein during nitrogen fixation, in addition to catalyzing MoFe protein-independent substrate (CO2) reduction and facilitating MoFe protein metallocluster biosynthesis.
evidence: This claim is supported by established scientific knowledge about nitrogenase function and is cited in the introduction with references (Thorneley and Lowe, 1983; Wolle et al., 1992; Rutledge and Tezcan, 2020).

claim: The nitrogenase Fe protein catalyzes MoFe protein-independent substrate (CO2) reduction.
source: The nitrogenase Fe protein mediates ATP-dependent electron transfer to the nitrogenase MoFe protein during nitrogen fixation, in addition to catalyzing MoFe protein-independent substrate (CO2) reduction and facilitating MoFe protein metallocluster biosynthesis.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work (Rebelein et al., 2017) as stated in the introduction.

claim: The nitrogenase Fe protein facilitates MoFe protein metallocluster biosynthesis.
source: The nitrogenase Fe protein mediates ATP-dependent electron transfer to the nitrogenase MoFe protein during nitrogen fixation, in addition to catalyzing MoFe protein-independent substrate (CO2) reduction and facilitating MoFe protein metallocluster biosynthesis.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations (Allen et al., 1993; Burén et al., 2020) as stated in the introduction.

claim: ATP-dependent chalcogenide exchange occurs at the Fe4S4 cluster of the nitrogenase Fe protein when potassium selenocyanate is used as the selenium source.
source: Herein, we report crystallographic data demonstrating ATP-dependent chalcogenide exchange at the Fe4S4 cluster of the nitrogenase Fe protein when potassium selenocyanate is used as the selenium source, an unexpected result as the Fe protein cluster is not traditionally perceived as a site of substrate binding within nitrogenase.
evidence: This claim is supported by crystallographic data presented in the manuscript, including anomalous diffraction data and structural refinement.

claim: The Fe protein cluster is not traditionally perceived as a site of substrate binding within nitrogenase.
source: Herein, we report crystallographic data demonstrating ATP-dependent chalcogenide exchange at the Fe4S4 cluster of the nitrogenase Fe protein when potassium selenocyanate is used as the selenium source, an unexpected result as the Fe protein cluster is not traditionally perceived as a site of substrate binding within nitrogenase.
evidence: This reflects established scientific knowledge about nitrogenase substrate binding sites.

claim: The Fe4S4 cluster of the Fe protein is capable of core substitution reactions under certain conditions.
source: The observed chalcogenide exchange illustrates that this Fe4S4 cluster is capable of core substitution reactions under certain conditions, adding to the Fe protein's repertoire of unique properties.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the crystallographic observations of chalcogenide exchange presented in the manuscript.

claim: The Fe protein cluster can span three oxidation states (2+/1+/0), unlike most Fe4S4 clusters in metalloproteins which adopt two oxidation states.
source: Unlike most Fe4S4 clusters in metalloproteins which adopt two oxidation states, the Fe protein cluster can span three oxidation states (2+/1+/0) (Watt and Reddy, 1994; Angove et al., 1997; Liu et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work (Watt and Reddy, 1994; Angove et al., 1997; Liu et al., 2014).

claim: Both MgATP- and MgADP binding to the Fe protein result in lower reduction potentials of the Fe4S4 cluster relative to the nucleotide-free state.
source: While both MgATP- and MgADP binding to the Fe protein result in lower reduction potentials of the Fe4S4 cluster relative to the nucleotide-free state (see Rutledge and Tezcan, 2020), only the MgATP-bound state of the protein in the 1+ state is susceptible to rapid and complete iron chelation with bipyridine or bathophenanthroline (Walker and Mortenson, 1974; Ljones and Burris, 1978; Hausinger and Howard, 1983; Anderson and Howard, 1984).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work (Rutledge and Tezcan, 2020).

claim: Only the MgATP-bound state of the Fe protein in the 1+ state is susceptible to rapid and complete iron chelation with bipyridine or bathophenanthroline.
source: While both MgATP- and MgADP binding to the Fe protein result in lower reduction potentials of the Fe4S4 cluster relative to the nucleotide-free state (see Rutledge and Tezcan, 2020), only the MgATP-bound state of the protein in the 1+ state is susceptible to rapid and complete iron chelation with bipyridine or bathophenanthroline (Walker and Mortenson, 1974; Ljones and Burris, 1978; Hausinger and Howard, 1983; Anderson and Howard, 1984).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work (Walker and Mortenson, 1974; Ljones and Burris, 1978; Hausinger and Howard, 1983; Anderson and Howard, 1984).

claim: In the absence of nucleotide, iron chelation of the Fe protein cluster is slow.
source: In the absence of nucleotide, iron chelation is slow, while MgADP inhibits chelation.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about Fe protein behavior, as discussed in the introduction.

claim: MgADP inhibits iron chelation of the Fe protein cluster.
source: In the absence of nucleotide, iron chelation is slow, while MgADP inhibits chelation.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about Fe protein behavior, as discussed in the introduction.

claim: The 2+ oxidized form of the Fe4S4 cluster undergoes ATP-dependent Fe chelation, yielding an intact Fe2S2 cluster.
source: Furthermore, the 2+ oxidized form of the Fe4S4 cluster undergoes ATP-dependent Fe chelation, yielding an intact Fe2S2 cluster (Anderson and Howard, 1984).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work (Anderson and Howard, 1984).

claim: The origins of the unusual properties of the Fe protein cluster may reflect the solvent accessibility of the cluster and its positioning at the dimer interface.
source: The origins of these unusual properties of the Fe protein cluster are not well understood, but may reflect the solvent accessibility of the cluster and its positioning at the dimer interface.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about possible explanations for observed properties.

claim: Potassium selenocyanate (KSeCN) is an alternative substrate for nitrogenase.
source: Key to this study was potassium selenocyanate (KSeCN), which like thiocyanate, is an alternative substrate for nitrogenase (Rasche and Seefeldt, 1997; Spatzal et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work (Rasche and Seefeldt, 1997; Spatzal et al., 2015).

claim: Se-incorporation occurred at the FeMo-cofactor under KSeCN turnover, but not at the P-cluster.
source: The observation that Se-incorporation occurred at the FeMo-cofactor under KSeCN turnover, but not at the P-cluster, supported this paradigm.
evidence: This claim refers to prior observations from the group's previous work (Spatzal et al., 2015).

claim: Under KSeCN turnover conditions, the sulfide ligands of the Fe4S4 cluster exchange with 'Se' from KSeCN to yield an intact Fe4X4 cluster (X = Se, S) with Se-incorporation at all chalcogenide sites.
source: Herein, using these conditions, we report a novel cluster conversion at the Fe protein in which the sulfide ligands of the Fe4S4 cluster exchange with 'Se' from KSeCN to yield an intact Fe4X4 cluster (X = Se, S) with Se-incorporation at all chalcogenide sites.
evidence: This claim is supported by crystallographic data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The generation of Fe4Se4-containing Fe proteins using apoproteins and a selenium source, iron source, and reductant has been reported.
source: While the generation of Fe4Se4-containing Fe proteins using apoproteins (proteins deficient in the native Fe4S4 cluster) and a (1) selenium source, iron source, and reductant or (2) with synthetic clusters has been reported (Hallenbeck et al., 2009; Solomon et al., 2022), the work described herein details a reaction distinct from reconstitution; namely, we report an exchange reaction under KSeCN turnover using native Fe4S4-containing Fe protein.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work (Hallenbeck et al., 2009; Solomon et al., 2022).

claim: The work described herein details an exchange reaction under KSeCN turnover using native Fe4S4-containing Fe protein, which is distinct from reconstitution.
source: While the generation of Fe4Se4-containing Fe proteins using apoproteins (proteins deficient in the native Fe4S4 cluster) and a (1) selenium source, iron source, and reductant or (2) with synthetic clusters has been reported (Hallenbeck et al., 2009; Solomon et al., 2022), the work described herein details a reaction distinct from reconstitution; namely, we report an exchange reaction under KSeCN turnover using native Fe4S4-containing Fe protein.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data presented in the manuscript showing Se-incorporation into native Fe protein.

claim: The crystal structure of the Se-incorporated Fe protein was determined at 1.51 Å resolution.
source: The crystal structure at 1.51 Å resolution of the Se-incorporated Fe protein isolated from this reaction mixture is shown in Figure 2.
evidence: This claim is supported by the crystallographic data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The crystal form of the Se-incorporated Fe protein is isomorphous to the previously reported MgADP-bound state of the Fe protein.
source: The crystal form is isomorphous to the previously reported MgADP-bound state of the Fe protein (Wenke et al., 2019b), with the Fe protein molecular twofold axis coincident with a crystallographic twofold axis so that the asymmetric unit contains one subunit and half the cluster.
evidence: This claim is supported by crystallographic analysis and citation to prior work (Wenke et al., 2019b).

claim: The asymmetric unit of the Se-incorporated Fe protein crystal contains one subunit and half the cluster.
source: The crystal form is isomorphous to the previously reported MgADP-bound state of the Fe protein (Wenke et al., 2019b), with the Fe protein molecular twofold axis coincident with a crystallographic twofold axis so that the asymmetric unit contains one subunit and half the cluster.
evidence: This claim is supported by crystallographic analysis.

claim: The unique Fe1 and Fe2 sites of the Fe protein cluster are coordinated to Cys 97A and Cys 132A, respectively.
source: The unique Fe1 and Fe2 sites are coordinated to Cys 97A and Cys 132A, respectively, while the unique chalcogenide sites 3 and 4 are buried and surface exposed, respectively.
evidence: This claim is supported by the crystal structure data.

claim: The unique chalcogenide sites 3 and 4 of the Fe protein cluster are buried and surface exposed, respectively.
source: The unique Fe1 and Fe2 sites are coordinated to Cys 97A and Cys 132A, respectively, while the unique chalcogenide sites 3 and 4 are buried and surface exposed, respectively.
evidence: This claim is supported by the crystal structure data.

claim: Well-defined density was observed at both chalcogenide positions of the Fe4S4 cluster in the double difference anomalous Fourier map (Δanom12,668 eV − Δanom12,643 eV).
source: Well-defined density was observed at both chalcogenide positions of the Fe4S4 cluster in the double difference anomalous Fourier map (Δanom12,668 eV − Δanom12,643 eV).
evidence: This claim is supported by the anomalous diffraction data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Modeling the cluster exclusively as either the Fe4S4 or Fe4Se4 form resulted in substantial positive or negative difference density in the corresponding Fobs − Fcalc difference Fourier maps, respectively.
source: Modeling the cluster exclusively as either the Fe4S4 or Fe4Se4 form resulted in substantial positive or negative difference density in the corresponding Fobs − Fcalc difference Fourier maps, respectively (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by crystallographic refinement data and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: B-factors with lower or higher values at the core chalcogenide positions, relative to the iron cluster positions, were observed when the cluster was modeled exclusively as the all-sulfide vs. all-selenide form.
source: Likewise, B-factors with lower or higher values at the core chalcogenide positions, relative to the iron cluster positions, were observed when the cluster was modeled exclusively as the all-sulfide vs. all-selenide form, suggesting an under- vs. over-modeling of electron density, respectively (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by crystallographic refinement data in Supplementary file 1.

claim: The buried X3 position exhibits a greater extent of Se-incorporation relative to the surface exposed X4 position.
source: The Se occupancies at the X3 and X4 positions are shown in Table 1, entry 1, with the buried X3 position exhibiting a greater extent of Se-incorporation relative to the surface exposed X4 position.
evidence: This claim is supported by the Se occupancy data presented in Table 1.

claim: Se-incorporation at the Fe protein cluster occurred in the absence of the MoFe protein.
source: Se-incorporation at the Fe protein cluster occurred in the absence of the MoFe protein as observed in the Δanom12,668 eV − Δanom12,643 eV difference Fourier map.
evidence: This claim is supported by crystallographic data from control experiments without MoFe protein.

claim: No signal corresponding to the S = 3/2 state of the FeMo-cofactor is observed in the EPR spectrum of the Fe protein used in the no MoFe protein control reaction.
source: To rule out small amounts of contaminating MoFe protein, an electron paramagnetic resonance (EPR) spectrum of the Fe protein used in the no MoFe protein control reaction was acquired (Figure 2—figure supplement 3); no signal corresponding to the S = 3/2 state of the FeMo-cofactor is observed.
evidence: This claim is supported by EPR spectroscopy data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: The Fe protein used in the control was subjected to acetylene turnover conditions with no added MoFe protein, and no ethylene formation was detected by gas chromatography.
source: Additionally, the Fe protein used in the control was subjected to acetylene turnover conditions with no added MoFe protein. No ethylene formation was detected by gas chromatography, consistent with the absence of the MoFe protein.
evidence: This claim is supported by gas chromatography data from the control experiment.

claim: Performing the no MoFe protein reaction at lower KSeCN concentrations (11 and 1 mM KSeCN) resulted in a significant decrease in the intensities of the anomalous signals corresponding to the chalcogenide positions.
source: Performing the no MoFe protein reaction at lower KSeCN concentrations (11 and 1 mM KSeCN) resulted in a significant decrease in the intensities of the anomalous signals corresponding to the chalcogenide positions in the higher energy (12,668 eV) anomalous difference Fourier map, reflecting less Se-incorporation at the cluster (Figure 2e, f and Table 1, entries 3 and 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by anomalous diffraction data shown in Figure 2 and Table 1.

claim: No Se-incorporation is observed when the Fe protein and KSeCN are the sole components of the reaction.
source: No Se-incorporation is observed in the anomalous difference Fourier map calculated from data collected at 12,668 eV, when the Fe protein and KSeCN are the sole components of the reaction (see Supplementary file 2, PDB ID 7TPY and Figure 2—figure supplement 2d).
evidence: This claim is supported by crystallographic data from control experiments shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2d.

claim: When MgADP and KSeCN, but no MoFe protein or ATP regeneration system, are mixed with the Fe protein, no Se-incorporation at the Fe4S4 cluster occurs.
source: Additionally, when MgADP and KSeCN, but no MoFe protein or ATP regeneration system, are mixed with the Fe protein, no Se-incorporation at the Fe4S4 cluster occurs (Supplementary file 2, PDB ID 7TPZ and Figure 2—figure supplement 2e).
evidence: This claim is supported by crystallographic data from control experiments shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2e.

claim: No density corresponding to -SeCN was observed when the MgADP-bound crystal form was soaked with KSeCN.
source: Finally, in an attempt to observe a potential ligand-bound form of the Fe4S4 cluster, the MgADP-bound crystal form was soaked with KSeCN; no density corresponding to -SeCN, either near the Fe4S4 cluster or anywhere else in the protein structure, was observed (Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by crystallographic data from soaking experiments shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4.

claim: The ability of iron–sulfur cluster containing metalloproteins to undergo a variety of cluster conversions and exchange reactions involving exogenous iron and sulfur species has been recognized since the pioneering work of Beinert.
source: The ability of iron–sulfur cluster containing metalloproteins to undergo a variety of cluster conversions and exchange reactions involving exogenous iron and sulfur species has been recognized since the pioneering work of Beinert (Kent et al., 1982; Kennedy et al., 1983; Kennedy et al., 1984; Holm and Lo, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work (Kent et al., 1982; Kennedy et al., 1983; Kennedy et al., 1984; Holm and Lo, 2016).

claim: Selenium can be used as a structural surrogate of sulfur for monitoring S-exchange in clusters.
source: An orthogonal method for monitoring S-exchange in clusters uses selenium as a structural surrogate of sulfur (Reynolds and Holm, 1981; Moulis and Meyer, 1982).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work (Reynolds and Holm, 1981; Moulis and Meyer, 1982).

claim: Under KSeCN turnover conditions, the Fe protein cluster and the two-coordinate sulfides of the FeMo-cofactor undergo Se-incorporation.
source: Our group's previously reported Se-incorporation results coupled with the results described herein highlight both the utility of this approach with nitrogenase and the selectivity of this process, under KSeCN turnover conditions. While the Fe protein cluster and the two-coordinate sulfides of the FeMo-cofactor undergo Se-incorporation, the P-cluster, which has been reported to undergo redox-dependent structural changes (Peters et al., 1997; Keable et al., 2018), has not yet been observed to undergo exchange of any of the constituent sulfides.
evidence: This claim is supported by the crystallographic data presented in this manuscript and prior work.

claim: The P-cluster has not yet been observed to undergo exchange of any of the constituent sulfides under KSeCN turnover conditions.
source: Our group's previously reported Se-incorporation results coupled with the results described herein highlight both the utility of this approach with nitrogenase and the selectivity of this process, under KSeCN turnover conditions. While the Fe protein cluster and the two-coordinate sulfides of the FeMo-cofactor undergo Se-incorporation, the P-cluster, which has been reported to undergo redox-dependent structural changes (Peters et al., 1997; Keable et al., 2018), has not yet been observed to undergo exchange of any of the constituent sulfides.
evidence: This claim is supported by the absence of Se-incorporation at the P-cluster in the crystallographic data.

claim: The P-cluster has been reported to undergo redox-dependent structural changes.
source: While the Fe protein cluster and the two-coordinate sulfides of the FeMo-cofactor undergo Se-incorporation, the P-cluster, which has been reported to undergo redox-dependent structural changes (Peters et al., 1997; Keable et al., 2018), has not yet been observed to undergo exchange of any of the constituent sulfides.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work (Peters et al., 1997; Keable et al., 2018).

claim: Se-incorporation at the Fe4S4 cluster is only observed in the presence of MgATP.
source: In line with the proposal that MgATP-binding results in a conformational change that renders the cluster more accessible to ligand binding relative to the nucleotide-free or MgADP-bound states (Lindahl et al., 1987), Se-incorporation at the Fe4S4 cluster is only observed in the presence of MgATP.
evidence: This claim is supported by the control experiments showing no Se-incorporation without ATP.

claim: MgATP-binding results in a conformational change that renders the Fe protein cluster more accessible to ligand binding relative to the nucleotide-free or MgADP-bound states.
source: In line with the proposal that MgATP-binding results in a conformational change that renders the cluster more accessible to ligand binding relative to the nucleotide-free or MgADP-bound states (Lindahl et al., 1987), Se-incorporation at the Fe4S4 cluster is only observed in the presence of MgATP.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work (Lindahl et al., 1987) and is consistent with the experimental observations.

claim: The accessibility of the Fe protein cluster contrasts with most Fe4S4-containing proteins that feature buried clusters.
source: The accessibility of the Fe protein cluster (Georgiadis et al., 1992; Meyer, 2008; Einsle and Rees, 2020) contrasts with most Fe4S4-containing proteins that feature buried clusters, with only a few exceptions (Georgiadis et al., 1992; Locher et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work (Georgiadis et al., 1992; Meyer, 2008; Einsle and Rees, 2020; Locher et al., 2001).

claim: Although the Fe protein cluster remains relatively exposed in the absence of nucleotide or in the presence of MgADP, incubation with KSeCN does not result in S/Se-exchange under these conditions.
source: It should be noted that although the Fe protein cluster remains relatively exposed in the absence of nucleotide or in the presence of MgADP (Figure 2a, b), incubation with KSeCN does not result in S/Se-exchange under these conditions (Figure 2—figure supplement 2d, e).
evidence: This claim is supported by crystallographic data shown in Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: The position of the cluster near the surface of the protein is not a sufficient condition for KSeCN-derived Se-incorporation.
source: Consequently, the position of the cluster near the surface of the protein is not a sufficient condition for KSeCN-derived Se-incorporation.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that surface exposure alone does not lead to Se-incorporation without ATP.

claim: The observations highlight the MgATP-dependent nature of the Fe protein as a means of regulating the physiological properties of the cluster and cluster atom exchange.
source: These observations highlight the MgATP-dependent nature of the Fe protein as a means of regulating the physiological properties of the cluster and cluster atom exchange.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental observations showing ATP-dependence of Se-incorporation.

claim: The ability of Fe protein to reduce CO2-to-CO suggests that the Fe4S4 cluster may coordinate CO2.
source: The ability of Fe protein to reduce CO2-to-CO (Rebelein et al., 2017), in the absence of the MoFe protein, suggests that the Fe4S4 cluster may coordinate CO2 (Rettberg et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is speculative, based on inference from the CO2 reduction activity and cited work (Rebelein et al., 2017; Rettberg et al., 2019).

claim: The first observed instance of N2 bound to a synthetic FeS cluster (a MoFe3S4 cubane) was recently reported.
source: Furthermore, the first observed instance of N2 bound to a synthetic FeS cluster (a MoFe3S4 cubane) was recently reported (McSkimming and Suess, 2021), demonstrating that relatively simple FeS clusters can coordinate exogenous ligands (Brown and Suess, 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work (McSkimming and Suess, 2021; Brown and Suess, 2022).

claim: Relatively simple FeS clusters can coordinate exogenous ligands.
source: Furthermore, the first observed instance of N2 bound to a synthetic FeS cluster (a MoFe3S4 cubane) was recently reported (McSkimming and Suess, 2021), demonstrating that relatively simple FeS clusters can coordinate exogenous ligands (Brown and Suess, 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work (McSkimming and Suess, 2021; Brown and Suess, 2022).

claim: KSeCN can be viewed as a substrate analog to CO2.
source: In the context of MoFe protein-independent CO2 reduction and ligand binding to synthetic clusters, KSeCN can be viewed as a substrate analog to CO2, with the Se-exchange mechanism proceeding by initial -SeCN binding to an Fe center, followed by Se–C bond cleavage, and chalcogenide exchange.
evidence: This is a speculative proposal about the mechanism of Se-incorporation.

claim: The Se-exchange mechanism may proceed by initial -SeCN binding to an Fe center, followed by Se–C bond cleavage, and chalcogenide exchange.
source: In the context of MoFe protein-independent CO2 reduction and ligand binding to synthetic clusters, KSeCN can be viewed as a substrate analog to CO2, with the Se-exchange mechanism proceeding by initial -SeCN binding to an Fe center, followed by Se–C bond cleavage, and chalcogenide exchange.
evidence: This is a speculative proposal about the mechanism of Se-incorporation.

claim: Ribbe et al. recently described the redox and catalytic properties of a fully Fe4Se4-reconstituted Fe protein.
source: Finally, while we have not probed the catalytic properties of the (partially) Se-incorporated Fe protein, Ribbe et al. recently described the redox and catalytic properties of a fully Fe4Se4-reconstituted Fe protein (Solomon et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work (Solomon et al., 2022).

claim: The Fe4Se4-reconstituted Fe protein exhibited poorer catalytic activity relative to the native protein.
source: In short, the Fe4Se4-reconstituted Fe protein exhibited poorer catalytic activity relative to the native protein (Solomon et al., 2022), which is consistent with the poor KSeCN reduction activity previously reported by our group given the likelihood that Se-incorporated Fe protein was also being generated under these conditions (Spatzal et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work (Solomon et al., 2022).

claim: Any future models of substrate reduction by nitrogenase should consider the possibility that the Fe protein cluster is noninnocent with respect to substrate binding.
source: As highlighted in this work, any future models of substrate reduction by nitrogenase should consider the possibility that the Fe protein cluster is noninnocent with respect to substrate binding.
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the findings of the manuscript.

claim: MoFe protein had a specific activity of 2940 ± 30 nmol min−1 mg−1 (Vmax) when measured by acetylene reduction at saturation.
source: MoFe protein had a specific activity of 2940 ± 30 nmol min−1 mg−1 (Vmax) and Fe protein had a specific activity of 1880 ± 90 nmol min−1 mg−1 (Vmax) when measured by acetylene reduction at saturation of each component.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental measurements of enzyme activity.

claim: Fe protein had a specific activity of 1880 ± 90 nmol min−1 mg−1 (Vmax) when measured by acetylene reduction at saturation.
source: MoFe protein had a specific activity of 2940 ± 30 nmol min−1 mg−1 (Vmax) and Fe protein had a specific activity of 1880 ± 90 nmol min−1 mg−1 (Vmax) when measured by acetylene reduction at saturation of each component.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental measurements of enzyme activity.

claim: The belt sulfides of the FeMo-cofactor were labile, with Se-incorporation predominantly at the 2B site, but also at the 5A and 3A sites.
source: Consistent with our previously published MoFe protein structures containing Se-incorporated FeMo-cofactor (Spatzal et al., 2015; Henthorn et al., 2019), this structure revealed that (1) the belt sulfides were labile, with Se-incorporation predominantly at the 2B site, but also at the 5A and 3A sites (Figure 2—figure supplement 5) and (2) no Se-incorporation occurs at the P-cluster.
evidence: This claim is supported by crystallographic data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 5 and citations to prior work (Spatzal et al., 2015; Henthorn et al., 2019).

claim: No Se-incorporation occurs at the P-cluster of the MoFe protein.
source: Consistent with our previously published MoFe protein structures containing Se-incorporated FeMo-cofactor (Spatzal et al., 2015; Henthorn et al., 2019), this structure revealed that (1) the belt sulfides were labile, with Se-incorporation predominantly at the 2B site, but also at the 5A and 3A sites (Figure 2—figure supplement 5) and (2) no Se-incorporation occurs at the P-cluster.
evidence: This claim is supported by crystallographic data and citations to prior work (Spatzal et al., 2015; Henthorn et al., 2019).

claim: The EPR spectrum of the Fe protein features an S = 1/2 signal corresponding to the [Fe4S4]1+ state of the cluster with g = [2.05, 1.94, 1.88].
source: The EPR spectrum of the Fe protein features an S = 1/2 signal corresponding to the [Fe4S4]1+ state of the cluster with g = [2.05, 1.94, 1.88] (Lindahl et al., 1987).
evidence: This claim is supported by EPR spectroscopy data and citation to prior work (Lindahl et al., 1987).

claim: The Fe protein can exist in the S = 3/2 and S = 1/2 states.
source: While the Fe protein can exist in the S = 3/2 and S = 1/2 states, the population of the spin state depends on the sample conditions, including the presence of nucleotide and solvent.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about Fe protein spin states.

claim: The population of the Fe protein spin state depends on the sample conditions, including the presence of nucleotide and solvent.
source: While the Fe protein can exist in the S = 3/2 and S = 1/2 states, the population of the spin state depends on the sample conditions, including the presence of nucleotide and solvent.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about Fe protein spin states.

claim: In 50% ethylene glycol, used as a cryoprotectant, most of the Fe protein cluster is in the S = 1/2 state.
source: In 50% ethylene glycol, used as a cryoprotectant, most of the Fe protein cluster is in the S = 1/2 state (Lindahl et al., 1985).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work (Lindahl et al., 1985).

claim: Based on the crystallographic data, the Se-labeled Fe protein exists in a mixture of Se-containing cluster states (i.e., Fe4S4, Fe4S3Se, Fe4S2Se2, Fe4SSe3, and Fe4Se4 may all be present).
source: Based on the crystallographic data, we anticipate that the Se-labeled Fe protein exists in a mixture of Se-containing cluster states (i.e., Fe4S4, Fe4S3Se, Fe4S2Se2, Fe4SSe3, and Fe4Se4 may all be present).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the crystallographic occupancy data.

claim: A familiar g = 2 signal corresponding to the [Fe4S4]1+ cluster of the Fe protein was observed in the EPR spectrum of the Se-labeled Fe protein.
source: As such, a familiar g = 2 signal corresponding to the [Fe4S4]1+ cluster of the Fe protein was observed (Figure 2—figure supplement 7).
evidence: This claim is supported by EPR spectroscopy data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 7.

claim: The signal of the -S/-Se mixture of the Fe protein cluster could be successfully simulated using the same parameters as the all-S-containing Fe protein cluster.
source: While there are slight differences in the EPR spectra between the all-S vs. Fe4X4 (X = S, Se) mixture of the Fe protein cluster, the signal of the -S/-Se mixture could be successfully simulated using the same parameters as the all-S-containing Fe protein cluster (Buscagan et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by EPR spectroscopy data and citation to prior work (Buscagan et al., 2021).

claim: EPR spectra of Fe4S4 vs. Fe4Se4 clusters are nearly identical.
source: One plausible interpretation of our EPR data is that the various Fe4X4 states yield nearly identical, overlapping, signals consistent with the observation that EPR spectra of Fe4S4 vs. Fe4Se4 clusters are nearly identical (Bobrik et al., 1978).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work (Bobrik et al., 1978).

claim: An Fe protein with an Fe4Se4 cluster is reduced to the all ferrous state in the presence of dithionite, rendering it EPR silent in perpendicular mode EPR.
source: Alternatively, it has been recently reported that an Fe protein with an Fe4Se4 cluster is reduced to the all ferrous state in the presence of dithionite, rendering it EPR silent in perpendicular mode EPR (Solomon et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work (Solomon et al., 2022).

claim: The FeMo-cofactor is traditionally perceived as the site of N2 (and other substrate) binding within nitrogenase.
source: Within nitrogenase, the FeMo-cofactor is traditionally perceived as the site of N2 (and other substrate) binding.
evidence: This reflects established scientific knowledge about nitrogenase substrate binding.

claim: Thiocyanate is an alternative substrate for nitrogenase.
source: Key to this study was potassium selenocyanate (KSeCN), which like thiocyanate, is an alternative substrate for nitrogenase (Rasche and Seefeldt, 1997; Spatzal et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is implied by the comparison of KSeCN to thiocyanate and is supported by citations.

claim: The Se-incorporated proteins were prepared using KSeCN turnover conditions that include KSeCN as the selenium source, dithionite as the reductant, and an ATP regenerating system.
source: We initially observed Se-incorporation into the Fe protein cluster using our group's previously reported KSeCN turnover conditions, which include KSeCN as the selenium source, dithionite as the reductant, and an ATP regenerating system (Mustafa and Mortenson, 1967; Spatzal et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim describes the experimental conditions used and is supported by citations to prior work (Mustafa and Mortenson, 1967; Spatzal et al., 2015).

claim: For the 22 mM KSeCN reaction with MoFe protein, the Se occupancy at the X3 position is 0.51 ± 0.09 and at the X4 position is 0.43 ± 0.06.
source: Table 1, entry 1
evidence: This claim is supported by the occupancy data presented in Table 1.

claim: For the 22 mM KSeCN reaction without MoFe protein, the Se occupancy at the X3 position is 0.58 ± 0.03 and at the X4 position is 0.38 ± 0.05.
source: Table 1, entry 2
evidence: This claim is supported by the occupancy data presented in Table 1.

claim: The mechanism of chalcogenide exchange at the Fe protein cluster remains open.
source: While the crystallographic observations described herein unambiguously establish the occurrence of chalcogenide exchange at the Fe protein cluster, the mechanism of this reaction remains open.
evidence: This is an explicit statement about the current state of knowledge.
